prayer.text: Saint Anthony of Egypt, pray for us.

cues.text: A Word Heard as if for the First Time

Born around 251 near Heracleopolis in Egypt to prosperous Christian parents, Anthony was left, while still a young man, the guardian of a considerable inheritance and of a younger sister after both his parents died.
Entering church one day not long after, he heard the Gospel words to the rich young man read aloud: go, sell what you have, and give to the poor, and come, follow me .
We are told that he received them not as words addressed to someone else long ago, but as words spoken directly and personally to himself.
This is the grace the Church has always prized in the saints: the capacity to hear familiar words of Scripture as if for the very first time, and to let them reorder an entire life on the spot.
Anthony gave away his lands, provided for his sister's care among a community of consecrated virgins, and set out to live the Gospel without reservation.
Into the Desert Alone
Anthony's ascetic path led him progressively further from human company: first to the edge of his own village under a local hermit's guidance.
He then sought greater isolation among the tombs outside town, and finally, around the year 285, crossed the Nile to Pispir.
There, at an abandoned Roman fort, he sealed himself in for some twenty years, receiving food over the wall and speaking to almost no one.
His biographer, St. Athanasius , later Bishop of Alexandria, came to know Anthony personally.
He does not shy from describing the desert combat these years involved.
Athanasius's account recounts relentless temptation, discouragement, and what he understood as direct assault by the demonic.
He met these trials again and again with prayer, fasting, and an unyielding trust that Christ himself stood at his side.
A Peace That Drew the World to Him
When Anthony finally emerged from his enclosure around the year 305, those who broke down the door expected to find a man wasted and broken by two decades of solitary struggle.
Instead, Athanasius tells us, they found him in sound health of body and, more strikingly still, entirely at peace and balanced in soul.
In the biographer's own words, he was a man guided by reason and abiding in a perfectly natural state.
Word of this extraordinary equilibrium spread quickly.

Disciples began to gather around him, drawn less by his teaching, at first, than by the simple, radiant evidence that a human life given wholly to God could achieve a wholeness the world's own comforts could never provide.
Father of a New Way of Life
Though Anthony himself never founded a formal monastic order in the organized sense that Pachomius would soon establish nearby, a loose community of hermits grew around his example.
Each lived apart, yet in loose fellowship and occasional common worship.
This community became the seedbed from which the whole tradition of Christian monasticism, East and West, would eventually grow.
Anthony ventured from his solitude only rarely and for grave cause.
Once, he encouraged the confessors of the faith during a renewed persecution.
Near the very end of his long life, he traveled to Alexandria at Athanasius's request to preach publicly against the Arian heresy.
A life of the deepest withdrawal from the world remained, when the Church's need was great enough, entirely at the world's service.
A Long Life Ended in Peace
Anthony died in 356, reputedly at the extraordinary age of one hundred and five, still active in spirit to the very end.
He had asked to be buried in a secret and unmarked grave, a final gesture of the same humility that had marked his whole life.
Even in death, he was unwilling to become an object of veneration that might distract from the God to whom his whole existence had pointed.
Legacy
Athanasius's Life of Anthony , written soon after the hermit's death, spread with astonishing speed across the Christian world.
Its account of one man's total, undivided surrender to God helped ignite the monastic movement that would soon reshape both the Eastern and Western Church.
St. Augustine himself later recorded how reading this very book moved two imperial officials in Trier to abandon worldly ambition altogether.

It was a chain of grace running directly from one Egyptian hermit's fidelity to the conversion of hearts he would never meet, a chain that, in truth, has never stopped extending, generation after generation, down to our own day.
